components.text: Whether the New Testament narratives provide sufficiently reliable historical access despite internal features and claimed confirmations.
Whether the New Testament narratives provide sufficiently reliable and accurate access to the alleged resurrection events.
Whether claimed eyewitness access, authorship, and external confirmations provide sufficiently reliable and independently corroborated historical sources.
Whether the particular resurrection testimony has the source quality needed to carry evidential weight, beyond testimony's general admissibility.
Whether claimed eyewitness access and external confirmation adequately establish the New Testament source foundation.
Whether testimony in this case has confirmed primary provenance and sufficient independent corroboration.
Whether Jesus's death and placement in the alleged tomb are independently established prerequisites for an empty-tomb resurrection inference.
Whether Jesus's death and prior placement in the alleged tomb are adequately established prerequisites for an empty-tomb inference.
Whether sincere costly conduct and claimed firsthand experience support the truth of resurrection rather than merely committed belief.
Whether reported appearance accounts reliably preserve accurate witness experiences rather than mistakes or later transmission distortions.
Whether apparent sincerity and costly conduct support the truth of firsthand resurrection experiences rather than sincere error.
Whether testimonial sincerity is sufficient for reliable transmission and factual accuracy.
Whether reported experiences remain reliable after possible mistake and later transmission distortion.
Whether a specific tomb existed, contained Jesus, and was later empty such that its emptiness requires comparative explanation.
Whether there is an independently established tomb that contained Jesus and was subsequently found empty.
Whether a high likelihood of reports under resurrection can establish a high posterior probability of resurrection given those reports.
Whether the proposed probability framework keeps likelihood direction distinct from posterior probability and incorporates priors and alternatives.
Whether a high likelihood of reports given resurrection is sufficient to establish a high probability of resurrection given those reports.
Whether the proposed probability framework keeps likelihood direction distinct from posterior probability.
Whether persecution, suffering, death, and strength of commitment establish the truth of the underlying resurrection belief.
Whether willingness to suffer or die establishes the truth of the resurrection belief rather than merely its sincerity.
Whether fitting divine purposes for incarnation and authentication materially raise or protect the prior probability of resurrection.
Whether fitting divine incarnation purposes raise the conditional prior probability of Jesus's resurrection.
Whether the weakness of particular competing explanations is sufficient to establish resurrection as the warranted comparative conclusion.
Whether the biblical accounts have adequate independent reliability before their contents can support a comparative resurrection inference.
Whether failure of selected natural alternatives is enough to warrant belief in resurrection under a comparative framework.
Whether the biblical accounts possess adequate independently confirmed reliability before alternatives are compared.
Whether weaknesses in hallucination or collusion explanations independently establish resurrection.
Whether the largest-probability member of an exhaustive hypothesis set must be believed when its evidential support remains insufficient.
Whether a qualitative probability framework permits rational suspension when data do not warrant reliable assignments or a sufficiently probable conclusion.
Whether the highest-ranked member of an exhaustive hypothesis set must be believed despite insufficient absolute evidential support.
Whether qualitative probability assignments warrant a conclusion when the available data remain insufficient.
